title: Trade, Wages, and the Political Economy of Trade Protection
research_question: How do reductions in trade protection affect the wages of workers employed in liberalized industries relative to workers in other sectors? Specifically, does lowering tariffs in an industry reduce the industry-specific component of wages earned by its workers, beyond any economy-wide changes in the returns to skill?
data_description: The study combines two main data sources for Colombia covering 1984-1998. Worker-level data come from the June waves of the Colombian National Household Survey (NHS) administered by DANE for 1984, 1986, 1988, 1990, 1992, 1994, 1996, and 1998, a repeated cross-section of urban workers (roughly 18,000-36,000 workers per year) reporting earnings, hours worked, demographics (age, gender, marital status, education, literacy), occupation, job type, formality (employer compliance with social security), workplace size and type, region, and 2-digit ISIC industry of employment (33 industries). Industry-level tariff data, provided by Colombia's National Planning Department (DNP), are available for 21 industries spanning agriculture, mining, manufacturing, and selected services. Supplementary data include nontariff barrier coverage ratios (1986, 1988, 1992), industry imports and exports, UNIDO gross fixed capital formation for manufacturing, the nominal effective exchange rate (IMF), and world coffee prices.
institutional_context: Colombia, which had not participated in earlier GATT tariff-reducing rounds, entered the 1980s with very high and highly dispersed tariffs, particularly in manufacturing, where average protection was about 50% and sectors such as textiles/apparel and wood products faced tariffs of 60-90%. Between 1985 and 1994, the country undertook drastic, staged trade liberalization, with major tariff cuts in 1985 and especially in 1990-1991, bringing average tariffs down to roughly 10% and substantially reducing nontariff barriers. Because liberalization was tied to WTO accession, the government targeted a near-uniform tariff of about 13% across industries, leaving little scope for industry-specific lobbying and implying that tariff reductions were proportional to pre-reform 1983 tariff levels. Pre-reform protection was concentrated in unskilled-labor-intensive sectors. The economy also featured rigid labor regulations, a large informal sector, and a 1990 labor market reform reducing hiring and firing costs.
